summary: Young children (about 4-6) compare which of two objects is heavier, first by HEFTING (holding one object in each hand) and then by confirming with a two-pan balance. The central aim is to challenge the 'bigger = heavier' assumption by deliberately pairing a small heavy object with a big light one, so size stops being a reliable guide. Children read the balance as 'the side that goes DOWN is heavier', use full comparative language (heavier than / lighter than), and progress to ordering three objects by pairwise comparison. At this stage 'mass' and 'weight' are used interchangeably. The curriculum frames this as a practical activity with real materials; screen or picture activities can support balance-reading and prediction but cannot deliver the felt sense of weight (no haptics).
misconceptions: Bigger = heavier — judges mass by size or appearance
The taller/longer/fuller object is heavier (conflates mass with another attribute)
Misreads the balance — thinks the RAISED pan is the heavier side
Expects to order objects by weight just by looking

activities.title: Heft then balance: feel it, then confirm
steps: Hold one object in each hand (heft) and say which feels heavier — try this with eyes shut so appearance can't guide the choice.

Pair a small heavy object (a metal weight or pebble) with a big light object (an empty plastic box or inflated balloon), checked beforehand on the balance so the small item really is heavier (a small pebble can be lighter than a large box). Predict which is heavier before touching.
Place both on a two-pan balance and watch which pan goes down; say 'the ____ is heavier than the ____' in a full sentence.
Repeat with several deliberately misleading pairs (e.g. big cushion vs small tin of beans), checked beforehand so the small item really is heavier, so that size is repeatedly the wrong guide.
Press gently on one pan with a hand to feel that pushing down harder on one side makes that pan go down, just as a heavier object does.
activities.insight: Weight is felt and measured, not seen — a small object can be heavier than a big one, and the balance settles cases your eyes cannot.

activities.title: Order three objects by weight
steps: Take three objects, including at least one small-heavy and one big-light item.
Compare them two at a time on the balance ('Is this heavier than that?'), using the balance outcome each time.
Arrange them lightest to heaviest based on the pairwise comparisons, not on how they look.
Describe the order aloud using 'heavier than' and 'lighter than'.
activities.insight: You can put objects in order of weight by comparing pairs, and the order may differ from what their sizes suggest.

activities.title: Virtual balance: predict then watch the beam tip (scaffold)
steps: Drag a small metal cube and a big foam block onto the two pans of a virtual two-pan balance; the objects are configured so the small dense cube genuinely outweighs the larger light block.
Predict which side will drop before releasing.
Watch the beam tip to reveal that the small cube wins, with running 'heavier/lighter' labels appearing on each side.
Try a round of deliberately misleading pairs (big cushion vs small tin), again set so the small heavy item is actually heavier.
Switch to an order-three-objects mode that works by successive balancing.
activities.insight: Reading a balance (down = heavier) and predicting outcomes can be practised on screen, and in this set-up (where the small object is actually heavier) the small-cube-wins surprise reinforces that size alone is not a reliable guide to weight.

activities.title: Balance-picture check (recognition)
steps: Look at a picture of a two-pan balance and say which object is heavier (the side tipped down).
Order a set of objects lightest-to-heaviest from a series of balance pictures.
Match objects to the balance outcome they would produce.
Answer a true/false claim read from a balance picture (e.g. 'the teddy is heavier than the car').
activities.insight: Once the physical idea is in place, you can interpret balance pictures: the lower pan holds the heavier object.

checkQuestion: Give the child a small heavy object (a metal weight or a pebble) and a large light object (a big empty plastic box or an inflated balloon), plus a third object, and a two-pan balance. Watch, don't quiz: (1) 'Hold one in each hand — which is heavier? How do you know?' (2) 'Now put them on the balance. Which is heavier? How can you tell from the scales?' (3) 'Put all three in order, lightest to heaviest.'
checkAnswer: Hefts and reports the small metal object as heavier despite being smaller (it presses down); on the balance names the pan that goes DOWN as the heavier one; orders the three by weight (not by size), using 'heavier than / lighter than'.
